d: A method for assessing a cross-border trade corridor: participants, flows, the cost stack, friction points, the last mile and the regulatory perimeter — with explicit notes on where reliable data ends and estimation begins.
b: Corridor intelligence Corridor intelligence. A corridor is not a market size. It is a set of named participants moving specific value under specific rules, and it can be described precisely if you ask the right questions in the right order. The method Most corridor analysis begins with a total addressable market and works down. That produces a number that cannot be acted on. Starting from the participants and working up produces a description that can be tested against reality. 1. Participants Who actually moves value on this corridor today? Name the banks, the payment institutions, the switches, the aggregators and the informal channels. If a corridor cannot be described in named institutions, the analysis is not yet real. 2. Flows Separate the flows that get bundled together: trade payments for goods, trade payments for services, intra-group treasury movement, personal remittance, and government or institutional transfers. They have different values, different frequencies, different documentation and different regulatory treatment. A statistic about one is not evidence about another. 3. The cost stack Cost is rarely a single fee. It is an origination fee, a conversion margin, intermediary charges, a receiving charge, and a set of costs that never appear on an invoice: working capital held against uncertainty, staff time spent reconciling, and delay in releasing goods. The visible fee is often the smaller half. 4. Friction points Where does a transaction on this corridor actually stop? Common answers include compliance holds on incomplete party data, currency unavailable at the size required, cut-off times missed across time zones, beneficiary details that fail validation at the last hop, and reference data lost between intermediaries. 5. The last mile How does value reach the beneficiary’s account domestically, through which licensed institution, on which rails, within which cut-off? Corridor propositions fail here more often than at settlement, and the last mile is the part that cannot be built remotely. 6. The regulatory perimeter Which activities on this corridor require authorisation, in which market, and who holds it? Which reporting obligations attach, and to whom? A corridor design that is elegant and unlicensable is not a design. What the data will and will not tell you Data availability for corridor analysis. Being explicit about the limits is part of the method. Question Data quality Caution Cost of sending personal remittances Reasonable. The World Bank’s Remittance Prices Worldwide publishes corridor-level pricing quarterly. It covers remittance products, not business payments. Applying it to B2B flows overstates or understates depending on size band. Value of recorded bilateral trade Reasonable. National statistics and UN Comtrade give recorded merchandise trade. d: Eko Infrastructure is operated by EKORails LTD, a company developing a compliance-first settlement and interoperability platform. Its regulatory status, what it is building and the relationship between the two platforms.
b: Disclosure EKORails LTD. The company that operates this research platform, what it is building, and exactly what its regulatory status is — stated here rather than left for a reader to discover. What EKORails is building EKORails LTD is developing a compliance-first settlement and interoperability platform designed to help regulated institutions and businesses move value across selected African and global trade corridors. In the terms used elsewhere on this site, it is being designed as an orchestration and record layer: it coordinates the sequence of a cross-border transaction, enforces agreed controls before an instruction is routed, and holds an append-only record of what happened. It is not designed to hold customer funds, act as principal in currency conversion, provide settlement finality or operate a payout licence — those functions remain with licensed institutions. The platform is in development. No capability is operating in production and no corridor is operating. Regulatory status EKORails LTD has applied to participate in the Central Bank of Nigeria Regulatory Sandbox. Participation and all proposed pilot activities remain subject to regulatory review and approval. EKORails LTD is not licensed, authorised, approved, endorsed or supervised by the Central Bank of Nigeria or by any other financial services regulator, and holds no payment services, banking, e-money or money transmission licence in any jurisdiction. The current stage-by-stage status is published on the EKORails regulatory pathway page and is only advanced when documentary evidence supports it. The relationship between the two platforms EKORails.com is the corporate and platform website: what the company is building, its regulatory pathway, its compliance framework and how to partner with it. EkoInfrastructure.com is the research, policy and market-intelligence platform. It explains the market rather than selling into it, and it is where the company’s claims about the market can be checked against sources. The separation is editorial, not legal: both are operated by EKORails LTD. What the separation buys a reader is that research pages are held to the editorial standards published here, and are not written to support commercial announcements. How we handle the conflict An operator with a commercial interest publishing research about its own market has a conflict. Three practices manage it, and they are checkable. Disclosure on every page. The footer of every page on this site states who operates it and what their regulatory status is. Fair treatment of alternatives. Where an existing system serves a corridor well, we say so — including where that makes the commercial case for EKORails weaker. Separate claim standards. Statements about EKORails’ own status and capability are held to a documentary evidence standard, reviewed by the named compliance officer before publication. If you think a piece here reads as advocacy rather than analysis, tell us at media@ekoin

d: Plain definitions of settlement and payments terminology: clearing, settlement, finality, nostro and vostro, RTGS, switch, corridor, correspondent banking, orchestration, stablecoin, ISO 20022 and more.
b: Reference Glossary. Terms that get used loosely, defined precisely. Where a term is contested or used differently across jurisdictions, we say so rather than picking the convenient meaning. A C D F I K L N O P R S T V A AML Anti-money laundering. The body of law, regulation and controls intended to prevent the financial system being used to launder the proceeds of crime. Authorised dealer An institution permitted by a central bank to deal in foreign exchange. The term and its scope vary by jurisdiction. C CFT Counter-financing of terrorism. Usually paired with AML in regulation and in a firm’s programme. Clearing The transmission, reconciliation and confirmation of payment instructions between institutions, and the calculation of the resulting obligations. Distinct from settlement. Correspondent banking An arrangement in which one bank holds an account for another so the second can reach a market where it has no presence. Corridor A directional pair of markets between which value moves — for example payments from market A to market B. A corridor has its own participants, rules, costs and frictions, and behaves differently in each direction. Cut-off time The time after which an instruction will be processed on the following business day in a given system or market. Cut-offs across time zones are a common and under-appreciated source of delay. D De-risking The withdrawal of correspondent or customer relationships by institutions judging the compliance cost or risk to be too high, rather than in response to a specific finding. Due diligence The verification and risk assessment a regulated institution performs on a customer or counterparty, at onboarding and on an ongoing basis. F Finality The point at which a transfer of value becomes irrevocable and unconditional. Defined by system rules and by governing law, not by how quickly a balance updates on a screen. FX spread The difference between the rate at which a party will buy a currency and the rate at which it will sell, or between the rate given to a customer and a reference rate. Compensation for holding and pricing currency risk. It can be moved or made visible; it cannot be conjured away. I Idempotency A property of an operation such that repeating it produces no additional effect. Essential in payments, where a retried instruction must never create a second payment. Interoperability The ability of separate systems to work together to complete a transaction end to end, including the data, rules and legal arrangements that make that possible — not only a technical connection. ISO 20022 An international standard for financial messaging that carries structured party, purpose and remittance data. Widely adopted, with staged migration across markets. K KYB Know your business. Verification of a business counterparty: legal existence, ownership, control and the nature of its activity. KYC Know your customer. Verification of a customer’s identity and risk profile. L Last mile The final leg

d: How payment activity is regulated across African markets: regulatory sandboxes and what they are not, licensing categories, AML and CFT expectations, sanctions, data protection and the policy architecture around cross-border payments.
b: Policy and regulation Policy and regulation. The regulatory architecture around cross-border payments, described as it is rather than as builders would prefer it to be. Regulation is the constraint that makes settlement infrastructure trustworthy, not an obstacle to route around. Regulatory sandboxes A sandbox is a supervised testing arrangement. A regulator permits a firm to test a defined proposition with a defined participant group, within limits — value caps, volume caps, a duration — and subject to reporting. The regulator retains the power to stop the test. Four things a sandbox is not, each of which is regularly misrepresented in market communications: It is not a commercial operating licence. It is not permission to serve the general public. It is not an endorsement, approval or recommendation of the firm by the regulator. It is not a guarantee that authorisation will follow. The distinction between applying to a sandbox, being admitted to one, and holding a licence is the single most commonly blurred line in this sector. A firm that has applied has done exactly that and nothing more. The operator of this platform, EKORails LTD, has applied to participate in the Central Bank of Nigeria Regulatory Sandbox. Participation and all proposed pilot activities remain subject to regulatory review and approval. Its current status is published at ekorails.com . Licensing categories Payment activity is not one licence. Different jurisdictions define different categories, and an entity commonly needs several, or needs partners who hold them. Categories that recur across African markets include payment service provider or payment solution service provider licences; international money transfer operator authorisations; switching and processing licences; e-money issuance; and banking licences. Two practical consequences follow. First, the question “are they licensed?” is incomplete without “for what activity, in which market?”. Second, an infrastructure layer that does not itself hold funds or convert currency may sit outside some categories entirely — but only if the boundary is genuinely maintained in the design, not merely in the marketing. [CONFIRM — current licensing category table by market, with regulator source and date] AML and CFT expectations The baseline is set internationally by the FATF Recommendations and implemented by national law and regulator guidance. In practice that means a documented risk assessment; customer and business due diligence proportionate to risk; sanctions screening; ongoing transaction monitoring; suspicious activity reporting; record keeping; a named responsible officer; training; and independent testing. For cross-border payments the requirement that most often bites is the transmission of complete originator and beneficiary information with the payment. t: Clearing versus settlement: the distinction that explains most cross-border confusion
d: Messaging, clearing, conversion, settlement and payout are five different functions performed by different parties under different rules. Separating them resolves most arguments about what a payment system does.
b: Settlement · Explainer Clearing versus settlement: the distinction that explains most cross-border confusion Messaging, clearing, conversion, settlement and payout are five different things, performed by different parties, under different rules. Most disagreements about what a payment system “does” dissolve once they are separated. By Eko Infrastructure editorial team Published [DATE] Last updated [DATE] 12 min read Source-checked Ask five people in a payments conversation what happens when money moves across a border and you will get five answers that are each partly right. That is not carelessness. It is because the phrase “a payment” bundles together at least five distinct functions, and different specialists have different ones in mind. Separating them is not pedantry. It determines which system is relevant to a given problem, which institution bears which risk, and whether a proposed improvement addresses the actual constraint or merely relocates it. The five functions Messaging is the transmission of a standardised instruction between institutions. It says who is paying whom, how much, in what currency, for what purpose, with what references. Messaging moves information, not value. Clearing is the reconciliation and confirmation of those instructions and the calculation of the resulting obligations. It establishes who owes what to whom. Clearing may net many instructions into a single obligation per participant per cycle. Conversion is the exchange of one currency for another at a price, performed by a party who holds both and takes a position. Conversion has a cost because holding and pricing currency risk has a cost. Settlement is the transfer of value that discharges the obligation, in an agreed settlement asset, between accounts the institutions recognise. Settlement is the moment the obligation is extinguished. Payout is the domestic credit to the beneficiary’s account, performed by a licensed institution on domestic rails within domestic cut-off times. Why the distinction matters commercially Consider a common complaint: “the payment took four days”. Which of the five functions consumed the four days? If it was messaging, the fix is a data or connectivity problem. If it was clearing, the answer may be a netting cycle that runs once a day by design. If it was compliance holds arising from incomplete party data in the message, the fix is upstream data quality, not a faster network. If it was conversion waiting on currency availability, no technology changes that. If it was payout arriving after a domestic cut-off, the constraint is a local operating window. Five different diagnoses, five different remedies, one symptom. A vendor who cannot say which one they address is not offering a solution; they are offering a slogan. b: Corridors · Method How to read a trade corridor: a method, and what the data will not tell you Corridor analysis usually starts with a market-size number and works down. That produces a figure nobody can act on. Starting from named participants and working up produces a description that can be tested. By Eko Infrastructure editorial team Published [DATE] Last updated [DATE] 11 min read Source-checked Why market-size analysis fails here A headline like “a two-hundred-billion-dollar market” is usually built by taking a broad trade or payments aggregate, applying a share, and applying a fee assumption. Each step is defensible on its own and the product is unusable, because the aggregate includes flows that are not addressable, the share is an assumption, and the fee varies by an order of magnitude across size bands. Worse, the number cannot be falsified. Nothing you observe on a real corridor will confirm or refute it, so it cannot guide a decision. Any market figure worth publishing shows its inputs, its assumptions and its arithmetic, and calls itself an estimate. The method Step 1 — Name the participants List the institutions that actually move value on this corridor: banks on both sides, payment institutions, switches, aggregators, and the informal channels that carry real volume whether or not anyone likes it. If you cannot name them, you do not yet have a corridor description. Step 2 — Separate the flows Trade payments for goods, trade payments for services, intra-group treasury movement, personal remittance and institutional transfers behave differently in value, frequency, documentation and regulatory treatment. Statistics about one are not evidence about another, and conflating them is the most common error in corridor decks. Step 3 — Build the cost stack Origination fee, conversion margin, intermediary charges, receiving charge — then the costs that never appear on an invoice: working capital held against timing uncertainty, staff time spent reconciling unmatched credits, and delay in releasing goods. For many businesses the invisible half is larger than the visible one, which is why fee-only comparisons mislead. Step 4 — Locate the friction Ask where transactions actually stop. Compliance holds from incomplete party data. Currency unavailable at size. Cut-offs missed across time zones. Beneficiary details failing validation at the last hop. Reference data lost between intermediaries. Each has a different remedy, and a proposition that does not name which one it addresses is not a proposition. Step 5 — Test the last mile How does value reach the beneficiary domestically — through which licensed institution, on which rails, within which window? This is where corridor propositions most often fail, because it cannot be built remotely and cannot be assumed. t: SWIFT is a messaging network: what that means for anyone comparing payment systems
d: SWIFT is routinely described as though it moves money. It does not. Understanding what it carries, and what banks do with what it carries, is a prerequisite for any serious comparison of settlement options.
b: Technology · Explainer SWIFT is a messaging network: what that means for anyone comparing payment systems “SWIFT takes three to five days” is one of the most repeated statements in fintech marketing, and one of the least examined. The network carries instructions. What happens to the value is a different question with a different answer for every route. By Eko Infrastructure editorial team Published [DATE] Last updated [DATE] 9 min read Source-checked What the network actually does SWIFT is a cooperative that operates a secure messaging network used by financial institutions to exchange standardised instructions. When a bank sends a payment instruction over it, what travels is a message: parties, identifiers, amount, currency, charges, purpose and references. Value does not travel over the network. Value moves through accounts the institutions hold with one another, with a shared correspondent, or with a central bank. The message tells the other institution what to do; the accounts are where it happens. Why the “three to five days” claim fails Once messaging and settlement are separated, the generalisation collapses. Between two banks with a direct relationship and aligned cut-offs, a payment may complete the same day. Through a chain of intermediaries, across time zones, with a compliance hold at one hop, it may take considerably longer. The determinants are the route, the currencies, the size, the time of day, the completeness of the data and the compliance outcome — not the messaging network. Presenting a worst case as a universal property of the network is a marketing device rather than an analysis. Eko Infrastructure does not publish it, and treats its use elsewhere as a signal about the publisher. It is also worth noting that the industry has invested substantially in tracking and speed for cross-border payments over the last decade, and that measured performance has changed as a result. Any claim about timing needs a date attached to it. [CONFIRM — current published performance data, with source and date] What actually causes delay Incomplete party data. Missing or malformed originator and beneficiary information triggers holds at downstream institutions, which is a data problem rather than a network problem. Screening review. A potential sanctions match requires human disposition, and correctly so. Cut-off times. An instruction arriving after a domestic cut-off waits for the next processing window, however fast it travelled. Currency availability. Conversion cannot complete if the currency is not obtainable at the required size. Chain length. Each additional intermediary adds its own checks, fees and windows. Four of these five persist regardless of which messaging or settlement technology is used. That is the point that matters for anyone evaluating a proposition: the proposition has to address the causes, not the symptom. t: What PAPSS does, where it operates, and where private platforms may complement it
d: A factual account of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System: what it was built to do, who participates, how settlement works, what it does not attempt, and where private-sector platforms may add something alongside it.
b: Policy · Explainer What PAPSS does, where it operates, and where private platforms may complement it The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is frequently invoked in market commentary and rarely described accurately. This is what it is, what it does, and what it does not attempt. By Eko Infrastructure editorial team Published [DATE] Last updated [DATE] 10 min read Source-checked Editorial position Eko Infrastructure is operated by a company building in the same market. We therefore hold ourselves to a specific standard on this subject: we describe PAPSS as its operators describe it, we do not characterise its adoption without a cited figure, and we do not present any product as a replacement for it. Where we make a judgement, we mark it as a judgement. What it is The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is a payment and settlement infrastructure developed with the African Export-Import Bank and African central banks. Its purpose is to enable payments between participating institutions across African markets in local currencies, with settlement arrangements involving participating central banks, rather than requiring every transaction to route through a currency and a correspondent outside the continent. The distinguishing idea is the settlement arrangement. If two institutions in different African markets can transact with each other in their own currencies, and the resulting positions are settled through an arrangement involving their central banks, the transaction does not require the traditional chain of foreign correspondents. [CONFIRM — precise operating model, from PAPSS official documentation] Who participates Participation runs through central banks and, beneath them, commercial banks and payment service providers in each participating market. A business does not use PAPSS directly; it uses its bank, which may or may not be connected. That structure has a direct consequence for anyone assessing a corridor: whether PAPSS is available for a given payment depends on whether both institutions in that specific transaction participate, not on whether their countries do. [CONFIRM — current participating central banks and institution counts, with source and date] What we do not say about it Commentary about PAPSS frequently asserts that adoption is negligible, or that a private-sector product is a “replacement play”. We do not publish either claim. The first requires a figure with a source, a period and a definition of what is being counted — instructions, value, connected institutions, active corridors. Those are different measures that give different answers, and a system built through central banks scales on a timeline that is not comparable to a consumer product. The second misdescribes the architecture. A system operating with central banks in an official capacity is not in the same category as a private orchestration layer, and framing it as a competitor tells you more about the person framing it than about the market

d: What settlement means, how clearing differs from settlement, how correspondent banking and FX liquidity work, what settlement finality is, and how stable-value settlement models are being discussed. Neutral, sourced explanations.
b: Settlement explained Settlement, explained. Six concepts that account for most of the confusion in cross-border payments. Each one is explained on its own terms, before any argument is made about what should be built. What settlement means Settlement is the discharge of an obligation between two parties by an actual transfer of value. When a bank in one country owes value to a bank in another, that obligation is settled when value moves between accounts the two institutions can each recognise as theirs — typically accounts held with each other, with a shared correspondent, or with a central bank. Everything else in a payment — the instruction, the compliance checks, the conversion, the statement entry the customer eventually sees — surrounds that moment. Confusing the surrounding activity with settlement itself is the most common error in market commentary, and it makes systems look like competitors when they are in fact doing different jobs. Clearing versus settlement Clearing is the transmission, reconciliation and confirmation of instructions, and the calculation of the resulting obligations. Settlement is the transfer of value that discharges them. A clearing process may net many instructions into a single obligation per participant per cycle, which reduces the value that must actually move. Settlement then happens once, for the net figure, in central bank money or another agreed settlement asset. A real-time gross settlement system takes the opposite approach: each instruction settles individually and immediately, removing netting risk at the cost of requiring more liquidity. Neither approach is better in the abstract. They trade liquidity efficiency against risk, and different systems choose different points on that trade. Full explainer: clearing versus settlement Correspondent banking A bank that has no presence in a market reaches it through a bank that does. The local bank holds an account for the foreign bank, and value moves between institutions by adjusting the balances on those accounts. The account the foreign bank holds abroad is its nostro; the same account, seen from the local bank’s side, is a vostro. The model works, and it carries an enormous share of world trade. Its costs are structural rather than incidental: each institution in a chain applies its own compliance requirements, holds its own liquidity, charges its own fees and provides its own cut-off times, and the originating customer sees the sum of all of them. Since the 2010s the number of correspondent relationships has declined in several regions as banks reassessed the risk and cost of maintaining them — a trend documented in work by the Financial Stability Board and the Bank for International Settlements. The consequence for affected corridors is fewer routes, not necessarily worse ones. d: The engineering behind payment policy: ISO 20022 and messaging standards, compliance architecture, transaction monitoring, auditability, data sovereignty and what distributed ledger designs do and do not change.
b: Technology Technology. Standards, architecture and evidence. The engineering questions that determine whether a settlement design can actually be supervised. Messaging standards Payment messages carry more than an amount. They carry the parties, their identifiers, the purpose, the charges and the references that let a beneficiary work out what the payment is for. When those fields are lost or truncated between systems, the consequences appear later as compliance holds and manual reconciliation. ISO 20022 is the standard the industry has converged on, and its value is precisely that it carries structured, extensible party and remittance data rather than free text. Migration across markets and systems has been staged over years, and coexistence with older formats is the normal condition rather than an exception. For anyone designing a corridor product, the practical question is not whether to support ISO 20022 but which fields survive each hop on the actual route, and what happens to a payment when one of them does not. [CONFIRM — current migration status by market and system, with source] Compliance architecture Compliance is an architectural property, not a department. Three design decisions determine whether a system can be supervised. Where controls run. Controls enforced before routing prevent bad instructions from entering the chain. Controls applied after the fact produce reports about payments that already left. What is recorded. Recording an outcome is not enough. Recording the rule version, the input data and the decision-maker is what allows a supervisor to ask about a past date and get an answer. Who owns the decision. In a chain of institutions, exactly one party must own each regulated decision. Designs that leave this ambiguous fail their first serious review. Transaction monitoring Monitoring compares activity against an expected pattern and raises alerts on deviation. Its engineering difficulties are well known: rules produce large numbers of false positives; thresholds that are too tight bury analysts and too loose miss activity; and tuning without versioning destroys the ability to explain past behaviour. Two claims should always be treated sceptically. First, that a monitoring system detects all illicit activity — none does. Second, that machine learning removes the need for explainability — supervisors ask why an alert was or was not raised, and a model that cannot answer creates a regulatory problem rather than solving one. Auditability An auditable system can answer, for any transaction and any date: what was known, what rule applied, who decided, when, and what happened next. That requires append-only records, versioned rules, time stamps from a trusted source, and retention for the longest applicable period across the markets involved.
